agree.reason: The honest A1C figures and the one-week trial would help with a wary reader, but this reader has quit three services before and gets no reason to believe this one will stick, such as no contract, cancel any time, meal swaps or a call with the dietitian.

honest.reason: The page drops the claim that the meals will lower A1C and reports 10 up, 3 flat and 1 up out of 14 honestly, but it invents 'less than most takeout' and 'enough protein and fiber to keep you full,' and it leaves out that medication changes weren't tracked.

works_the_facts.reason: It works out $12.90 per meal, but it never turns 37 of 88 into about 42% staying past six months, never notes the 14 are a small self-selected group, and leaves the trial-week value vague.

right_comparison.reason: The only comparison is an unsupported line about takeout, and the page never sets itself against cooking at home or the apps and services this reader already dropped.

qualification.reason: 'I can't promise any specific result' and the see-your-doctor note are fair hedges, but neither gives anything the reader can check, and the untracked medication changes that could explain the A1C drops go unmentioned.

objections.reason: The main objection, that the reader always quits within two months, is touched only by the retention figure, while no contract, skipping or cancelling any time, 6 swap choices, a 4-week menu cycle and a 15-minute call with the dietitian are all missing.

fit.reason: It is a sales page of about 400 words with clear sections and a trial-week button, though it leaves out practical details such as the delivery radius and the Thursday order cutoff.
